Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Don’t ask about anyone’s own use, and say “an adult you trust,” since home may not be the safe call. State driving and drinking laws are in the notes, not on the slides.

Every student in the room

"My parents would never" and faith are real reasons, families draw different lines, and not everyone has a ride, so the train or another family's driver counts.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Open plainly: “Today isn’t about scaring you. It’s about the five seconds after someone says ‘you coming?’”

Slide 2 · Notes

Hands up: 2? 5? 8? Don’t correct anyone. The next slide shows the answer.

Slide 3 · Notes

Ask: “Why does it feel like everyone does?” Then: when you guess high, you feel more pressure. The real number is on your side.

Slide 4 · Notes

Ask: “What changed? Not the rules. Just who was watching.” Friends make the reward feel bigger.

Slide 5 · Notes

The good news: the part of you that says no is still there in the moment. Give it a head start.

Slide 6 · Notes

Walk the five signs quickly. The first one matters most: people who decide ahead say no more easily and feel less awkward doing it.

Slide 7 · Notes

Two minutes, then switch. Ask: “What made the third ‘no’ easier or harder than the first?”

Slide 8 · Notes

Let them argue it first. Notes only: in Massachusetts, a junior operator can’t carry passengers under 18 (except family) for the first six months.

Slide 9 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 10 · Notes

Ask: “What would you actually say? Out loud, right now.” Keep the never-ride rule plain and calm.

Slide 11 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 12 · Notes

Ask: “How do you say no here and still be a good friend?” Saying no to the thing isn’t saying no to the person.

Slide 13 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 14 · Notes

Ask: “Who could be your person? An older sibling, an aunt, a coach, a neighbor?” Set it up this week, before you need it.

Slide 15 · Notes

Private, nobody shares: “What’s a reason you already have?” Some reasons are visible, some aren’t. All of them count.

Slide 16 · Notes

Keep it calm and short. Name the counselors by name. Most states have Good Samaritan protections for calling 911 in an emergency; details in the take-home.

Slide 17 · Notes

Turn and talk. Then ask: “Where else in your life does this show up?” Nobody speaks for a group.

Slide 18 · Notes

Give a minute of quiet writing. Share the take-home after: the five signs, the code word setup, who to call.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain why no feels harder with friends watching (the reward signal gets louder, the brakes still work), notice that most peers are less into risky plans than they look, and practice a short no, a swap and a code-word exit. The skill is planning ahead. Nobody should feel judged for a yes they already said.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 5 minGuess first, then the real number
  2. 6 minFriends turn up the gas; they don’t cut the brakes
  3. 5 minMake the call before the moment
  4. 6 min“Nah, I’m good” (pairs)
  5. 8 minThree moments, one per slide
  6. 4 minSet up a code word; when to get an adult now
  7. 6 minEvery reason counts, where else this shows up, and the close

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

The guess and the answer, gas and brakes, the five signs, one of the three moments, the code word, and the close. Share the take-home link afterward.

Before you teach
Don't ask about anyone's use.

No hands up about drinking, parties or rides. Some students in the room have already said yes to things, and some have a family member who struggles with alcohol or drugs. Talk about the skill, never about who did what.

Skip the lecture.

The lesson itself says lecturing friends backfires, and the same goes for us. Keep the tone practical. A student who said yes last weekend should leave with a plan and without shame.

Sexual pressure and photos.

The page names requests for nude or sexual photos as a hard no to tell an adult about. If a student discloses pressure, threats or a photo already sent, thank them, don't ask for details in class, and walk them to a counselor that day. Know your reporting duty before class.

If a friend is in trouble.

If a student says a friend is in trouble with alcohol or drugs, say you want to get help, not get anyone in trouble. Walk them to a counselor that day. Massachusetts' Good Samaritan law protects the caller and the person who overdosed from possession charges.

The car matters now.

Ninth graders ride with older students who just got licenses. Be clear on the hard line: never ride with someone who has been drinking or using, no matter how short the drive. A code-word call is always okay.

The code word may not be a parent.

Don't say "text your mom or dad." For some students home wouldn't be a calm place to make that call. Say "an adult you trust" and give examples: an older sibling or cousin, an aunt, a coach, a family friend.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Families draw different lines.

Rules about parties, curfews, rides and alcohol vary a lot from home to home, and so does what's allowed at family events. Teach the skill of saying no to what you've decided against, without ranking anyone's family rules.

"My parents would never" is a real reason.

For many students it's simply true, and saying so isn't weak. Faith is a real reason too, and so is a job, a coach or a game in the morning. Don't assume students are religious or that they aren't.

Who the trusted adult is.

Students live with a single parent, grandparents, two moms or two dads, foster or kinship families, or split time between homes. The code-word plan works with any adult they trust, including someone outside the home.

LGBTQ+ students and pressure.

Pressure can include being pushed to talk about who you like, or the threat of being outed. A student who isn't out may not have a safe adult at home for the code word. A counselor can help them figure out who.

Scripts help students who freeze.

Students who are autistic, anxious or slower to process often find a ready-made line easier than thinking on the spot. That's the point of deciding ahead. In the pair practice, let students write or read their line instead of performing it, and don't treat eye contact as a sign of confidence.

Not everyone has a ride.

Some families don't have a car or a parent free at night. In the Ayesha scenario, the train or another family's driver counts. "I open at work tomorrow" is a real reason for students with jobs.

What the research says

Teens, young adults and adults played a driving game alone and while they believed friends were watching. Only the teens took more chances with friends watching, and only the teens' reward regions lit up more. Their brake regions didn't get weaker.

Chein et al., Developmental Science, 2011 (Temple University)

306 people randomly assigned to work with two same-age peers took more risks and focused more on benefits than costs. The effect was strongest for ages 13 to 16 and 18 to 22, and weakest for adults 24 and older.

Gardner and Steinberg, Developmental Psychology, 2005

Princeton students believed they were more uncomfortable with campus drinking than the average student. Most of them felt that way, so the "average student" they imagined barely existed (pluralistic ignorance).

Prentice and Miller, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1993

About 29% of U.S. high school students reported current alcohol use, marijuana use or prescription opioid misuse in 2021. About 7 in 10 had done none of those in the past month.

CDC Youth Risk Behavior Survey, 2021 (Hoots et al., MMWR, 2023)

In five experiments with more than 2,000 people, those turning down an invitation expected the inviter to be far more upset, and far less likely to ask again, than inviters actually were. The reason for saying no was held constant, and results may differ across cultures.

Givi and Kirk, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2024

A 17-year-old driver's risk of dying per trip was about 1.5 times higher with one passenger, 2.6 times with two, and about 3 times with three or more, compared with driving alone. The pattern held for 16-year-olds.

Chen et al., JAMA, 2000

Massachusetts junior operators can't carry passengers under 18 who aren't immediate family for the first six months, unless a licensed driver 21 or older with a year of experience sits beside them. The Good Samaritan law protects a person who calls for help during an overdose, and the person who overdosed, from possession charges.

Massachusetts General Laws c. 90, § 8; c. 94C, § 34A
